title: Multi-Agent AI Orchestration Architectures: Five Coordination Models Compared
meta: How centralized, hierarchical, mesh, blackboard and contract-net orchestration compare for LLM agents, with a selection method, metrics and governance controls.

author.name: Quak Foo Lee
author.division: Division of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning

abstract: Choosing a multi-agent architecture is not simply a matter of adding more language-model agents. The architect must decide who owns a task, how work is assigned, where intermediate state is kept, which agents may communicate, and who is authorized to release the outcome. This paper compares five practical models (centralized orchestrator, hierarchical orchestration, decentralized mesh, shared blackboard, and market-based contract net) through their control paths, communication mechanisms, engineering trade-offs, and failure modes. A key distinction is that these labels describe different architectural dimensions: the first three principally describe control topology, whereas blackboard and contract net specify information sharing and task allocation mechanisms. Therefore, real deployments often combine them. The paper introduces a selection method, illustrative latency and coordination models, two advisory and engineering examples, and a deployment checklist. It makes no universal claim that distributed or bidding architectures are inherently more scalable or reliable; those properties must be demonstrated by workload-specific evaluation, persistence, access control, recovery, and governance.

sections.title: Introduction: Architecture Is a Control Decision

blocks.p: Modern agent platforms make it relatively easy to invoke several specialized agents for research, analysis, drafting, coding, validation, or action. The real engineering challenge begins when those agents must cooperate under latency, cost, security, and accuracy constraints. A weak design may duplicate research, lose evidence through repeated summaries, expose excessive tool permissions, or fail to terminate a debate. An elaborate topology is not automatically better than a capable single agent with a few tools.

An earlier paper in this journal, Multi-Agent AI Systems: Architectures, Coordination Patterns and Failure Modes, reviewed the foundational literature, empirical evidence, and broader failure taxonomy [1]. This companion paper narrows the focus to a practical question: How should an engineer select and implement the orchestration and coordination model for a specific workload? It follows the five approaches in Figure 1, then identifies the conditions under which each creates value and the controls necessary to make the design production-worthy.

The five labels are not a mutually exclusive set of software products. An orchestrator can assign tasks through a bidding mechanism; a hierarchy can publish artifacts to a shared blackboard; a mesh of agents can still require human approval for consequential actions. The chosen architecture should be expressed as an explicit combination of decisions, not inferred from a single marketing diagram.
Orchestration determines which actor runs next, what it may do, and how work transitions to a finished result. Four separate design questions are especially important (Table 1).

blocks.p: Figure 1 places the five models side by side and steps through how a task moves in each. To avoid misleading comparisons, this paper treats control location, state ownership, communication volume, and failure recovery separately. This aligns with modern frameworks that distinguish manager-style delegation, agent-to-agent handoffs, deterministic workflow routing, concurrent execution, and adaptive planners [2–6].

sections.title: The Five Approaches in Engineering Detail

blocks.p: A lead orchestrator receives the user's goal, decomposes it into subtasks, selects specialists, monitors the work, and produces or authorizes a synthesis. Worker agents generally return results to the lead rather than contacting one another directly. This creates a star-shaped control path, often with parallel worker execution. OpenAI documents manager-style agent-as-tool orchestration, and Anthropic reports an orchestrator–worker architecture for open-ended research [2, 4].

Advantages. The architecture has an unambiguous owner for task completion, a clear location for validation, and straightforward routing and auditability. Worker contexts can remain narrow, reducing irrelevant instructions and limiting inadvertent information sharing. It is a strong starting point for SME advisory, regulated reporting, and research synthesis.

Risks. The lead can become a throughput bottleneck or an information-loss point if every result is condensed into its context. A mistaken decomposition can cause all specialists to work on the wrong objective. A failure of the lead process can strand work unless the task ledger, artifacts, and permissions are recoverable.

Design controls. Use typed task contracts, a durable work ledger, timeouts and retry budgets, artifact references rather than long transcript replays, independent quality checks, and a separately enforced authorization layer. A logical single leader need not be a physical single point of failure if control state is checkpointed and workers are idempotent.

blocks.h3: 3.2 Hierarchical orchestration: nested responsibility at scale

blocks.p: A hierarchy adds supervisors for work domains or organizational tiers. For example, a top-level program orchestrator can delegate a technical workstream to an Engineering Supervisor and a financial workstream to a Commercial Supervisor; each supervises its own specialist agents. Amazon Bedrock Agents Classic documents a supervisor-and-collaborator form, while Microsoft describes adaptive manager-based orchestration [5, 7]. Implementation status matters: at the time of writing, Amazon states that Bedrock Agents Classic is not open to new customers, so it should not be assumed to be a current greenfield choice [8].

Advantages. Subdomain expertise, permissions, and budget limits can be localized. A manager can shield the upper tier from routine operational details. The model is useful when distinct teams require different validation rules or when a project naturally decomposes into separate accountable domains.

Risks. Each layer adds routing overhead, possibly another LLM call, and opportunities for context compression errors. Role ambiguity can produce conflicting orders; a deeply nested structure can hide the origin of unsupported claims.

Design controls. Set an explicit maximum delegation depth; assign one owner to each work package; preserve source artifacts across layers; require trace identifiers and structured summaries; and test both cross-domain disagreements and supervisor failures. Hierarchy should be justified by genuine domain boundaries, not by the mere size of an agent roster.

In a mesh, authorized peers may send work or evidence directly to one another and coordinate through a common protocol. This differs from a manager retaining all control. Peer handoffs in the OpenAI SDK transfer active responsibility to another specialist, although handoff-based routing is not necessarily a full mesh [2, 9]. At larger scale, interoperation standards such as the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol address communication across agent implementations and vendors [10].

Advantages. Meshes can support locally informed decisions, dynamic routing, and heterogeneous specialists. They may suit distributed monitoring, agent-to-agent service collaboration, and environments where there is no natural central decision-maker.

Risks. Unrestricted peer communication causes high message volume, ambiguous ownership, circular delegation, contradictory state, and difficult provenance. A logical lack of central leader does not by itself guarantee availability: peers may still share a database, model API, identity provider, or network dependency.

Design controls. Enforce authenticated agent identity, capability discovery, message schemas, correlation IDs, bounded hop counts, global termination rules, conflict resolution, and a system of record. Where decisions have safety or commercial consequences, separate peer recommendations from authorized external actions.

blocks.h3: 3.4 Blackboard coordination: agents collaborate through shared state

blocks.p: A blackboard is a versioned workspace that contains hypotheses, facts, partial results, tasks, and evidence. Rather than sending every result directly to every peer, a specialist reads relevant state, contributes an artifact or update, and notifies other subscribers. The concept predates LLM agents: Nii's account of blackboard systems traces the architecture to Hearsay-II and the independent knowledge sources that cooperatively solved problems through a shared workspace [11]. Later work treated the control problem, deciding which knowledge source acts next, as a blackboard problem in its own right [12].

Advantages. A shared evidence ledger improves discoverability and avoids repeatedly copying the same source across messages. It can integrate heterogeneous agents whose execution order is opportunistic. This makes it suitable for long-running research, engineering design reviews, and multidisciplinary knowledge work.

Risks. The blackboard can become a shared failure and contamination point. Stale records, conflicting writes, poisoned evidence, weak provenance, and accidental cross-project disclosure can propagate rapidly. Publish–subscribe notifications do not automatically make the state consistent or durable; for example, NATS distinguishes transient Core NATS messaging from persisted JetStream delivery [13].

Design controls. Use versioned schemas, immutable evidence references, optimistic concurrency or locking where necessary, role-based write permissions, data classification, retention rules, event ordering, and retraction/correction procedures. Treat retrieved documents and peer notes as untrusted data until verified.

blocks.h3: 3.5 Market-based or contract-net allocation: agents bid for work

blocks.p: Contract-net coordination distributes tasks through an explicit negotiation: a manager or announcing agent advertises a work package; prospective contractors assess their capability and availability; one or more bids are evaluated; and the task is awarded. Reid G. Smith formalized this mechanism in the 1980 contract net protocol as a way to coordinate nodes in distributed problem solving [14].

Advantages. Bidding can be useful when agents differ in skill, tool access, cost, queue length, geographic location, or resource availability. It permits dynamic assignment instead of hard-coded ownership and may improve allocation under changing workloads—if the bids reflect meaningful performance and cost information.

Risks. The auction itself adds delay, messages, and decision rules. Self-reported cost and confidence may be unreliable; a bidder might accept work it cannot complete. Task awards can be duplicated or abandoned, while unconstrained bids can optimize price at the expense of quality and safety. A contract-net mechanism can still have a central announcer, so it is not automatically decentralized or fault-tolerant.

Design controls. Specify task requirements and objective bid fields; validate eligibility before comparing bids; use deadlines and reserve options; record award decisions; constrain budget and tool authority; and provide reassignment and dispute paths. Treat bidding as an allocation protocol, not as a guarantee of autonomous intelligence or resilience.

The summary below gives conditional engineering observations rather than universal rankings. The meaning of high scalability or fault tolerance depends on state management, fault isolation, workload shape, network architecture, and recovery procedures.

blocks.p: The comparison in Table 2 summarizes these observations.

A centralized orchestrator plus blackboard is frequently more practical than a pure mesh: the orchestrator keeps final accountability while specialists write directly to a governed evidence store. A hierarchical orchestrator plus contract-net allocation can reserve bidding for an expensive specialist pool while retaining domain-specific approvals. These hybrids are often more precise descriptions than a single topology label; Figure 2 treats each axis as its own decision.

fig.caption: An architecture decision map. Control topology, information sharing, task allocation and workflow execution are independent decisions. The example hybrid combines a responsible supervisor, a versioned blackboard, selective capability bidding and bounded parallel work; it is an engineering illustration, not an industry standard.
fig.alt: Four horizontal bands, one per architectural axis (control topology, information exchange, task allocation, workflow scheduling), each listing its options, with arrows converging on an example hybrid design at the bottom.

blocks.p: Begin with the single-agent baseline. Use one agent plus tools and a deterministic workflow when tasks are short, role boundaries are artificial, source material is limited, or the output can be verified without multiple independent specialties. Anthropic recommends introducing complexity only when a simpler design falls short, and OpenAI's orchestration guidance explicitly distinguishes code-defined control flow from LLM-decided routing [2, 3].
If multi-agent work is justified, apply the following gates:

list: Accountability. Is there one owner for the final deliverable and one authority for release? For regulated or advisory work, default to an explicit lead.

Decomposition. Are there genuinely distinct domains with different inputs, methods, or permissions? If yes, bounded specialists help; nested management is justified only where subdomains need their own coordination.
State. Do multiple specialists need to inspect and revise the same hypotheses, records, or calculation artifacts? If yes, add a governed blackboard rather than broadcasting full transcripts.
Allocation. Does specialist availability or cost vary enough to warrant bidding? If not, fixed routing is easier to test and operate.
Concurrency. Are tasks independent enough to run simultaneously? Prefer parallel execution for independent work and sequential or gated stages for dependent work.
Consequence. Can agents write records, spend money, send messages, or affect safety-related operations? Use independent enforcement and human approval where required, regardless of topology.

blocks.p: Suggested default: For a professional services or SME analysis workflow, start with a single accountable orchestrator, two to four narrowly scoped specialists, a shared evidence repository, and an independent verification/release gate. Add a hierarchy, mesh or bidding mechanism only after measurement demonstrates a need. This is a design recommendation, not an experimentally established optimum.

sections.title: Latency, Message Volume, and Reliability Models

blocks.p: Topology changes the critical path more reliably than it predicts intelligence. Consider three independent specialists with observed execution times of 8, 10, and 12 seconds, plus 3 seconds of planning and 4 seconds of synthesis. With no queueing, contention, retries, or rate-limit delay, a serial workflow would take approximately 37 seconds, whereas parallel workers would finish in 19 seconds. The improvement comes from overlapping independent tasks, not simply from having multiple agents.

Applying Eq. (1) and Eq. (2) to the three workers, with coordination time neglected, gives 3 + 8 + 10 + 12 + 4 = 37 seconds serial versus 3 + 12 + 4 = 19 seconds parallel. In real operation, total time may be longer due to tool quotas, network costs, wait-for-all joins, validation, and straggler handling.

Communication cost requires separate treatment. A fully connected directed mesh of N agents has up to N(N − 1) potential one-to-one communication links; the equivalent undirected count is N(N − 1)/2. This counts possible relationships, not the number of messages actually exchanged. A lead-to-worker star has O(N) direct relationships, but messages can still proliferate if the orchestrator repeatedly broadcasts instructions or gathers iterative responses. Publish–subscribe may reduce explicit point-to-point coupling while increasing event fan-out if topics are poorly scoped.

Reliability is not a topology label. If every required stage in a series must independently succeed with probability p, an idealized k-stage chain has success probability pk. Real agent errors are correlated; external verification, replay and retry alter the result. A system with a physically replicated coordinator and durable state may recover better than a nominally decentralized mesh that depends on one unavailable datastore. Architecture must be measured by accepted-result rate, recovery time and controlled failure behavior, not by the count of agent nodes.

sections.title: Governance and Failure Modes Across All Models

blocks.p: A useful architecture review asks how the system behaves when a member produces incorrect information, a tool times out, an external document contains adversarial instructions, or one agent refuses to yield control. Framework routing by itself is not a security boundary. OWASP flags prompt injection and excessive agency as major LLM application risks; those risks can propagate through peer messages or shared knowledge stores [15].

blocks.p: Table 3 lists the failure scenarios a review should rehearse and the controls that contain them.

In particular, the decision to perform a tool action must be separated from the authority to perform it. For instance, an agent may recommend sending a supplier request, but an application-level policy and approval gate should determine whether any email is actually sent. Likewise, a design-review agent may recommend a process setpoint change, but should not have permission to modify control equipment. A trustworthy multi-agent harness maintains access rules, stable identity, telemetry, budgets, state transition controls, and recoverable side-effect records regardless of the communication graph.

blocks.h3: 8.1 SME ERP/WMS vendor selection: controlled research and comparison

blocks.p: Consider a hypothetical wholesale distributor selecting an inventory and warehouse management system. The project involves requirements discovery, vendor research, integration analysis, total-cost-of-ownership estimates, and a final recommendation. Evidence and approval are more important than unconstrained agent-to-agent negotiation.

Recommended hybrid: a centralized project orchestrator owns task definitions and the client-facing result; Research, Integration, Financial Analysis, and Risk Review agents operate on bounded subtasks; and a versioned evidence blackboard holds vendor claims, source links, assumptions, and evaluation tables. Independent vendor checks can run in parallel, but final scoring follows a deterministic rubric. A Review Agent verifies material claims, and a human consultant approves release. Contract-net bidding would add little if the four roles and resource pool are stable.

Testable acceptance criteria include complete source links for material vendor claims, a reconciled three-year cost table, explicit integration unknowns, and a final shortlist that does not silently convert an undocumented claim into an endorsed capability. This illustrates why central accountability and shared evidence often coexist.

blocks.h3: 8.2 Process-engineering feasibility review: specialists with release gates

blocks.p: For a hypothetical process plant feasibility study, assign specialists to mass and energy balances, equipment sizing, process-safety review, and cost assumptions. An Engineering Supervisor owns engineering consistency; a Commercial Supervisor handles cost estimation; both report to a Program Orchestrator. Shared artifacts are tagged with units, versions, calculation basis, and evidence status.

This is hierarchical control with shared-state coordination, not simply a tree of chat messages. A safety reviewer can flag a disputed temperature or materials constraint, but the final decision must pass a documented engineering approval gate. Unknown thermophysical data and unsupported vendor ratings remain open issues. No agent is authorized to alter plant operations. A mesh could be useful for communicating observations among monitoring agents, but is not necessary for approving a design basis.
Both examples are illustrative architecture scenarios, not descriptions of deployed client systems or measured case-study outcomes.

sections.title: Implementation Blueprint: From Diagram to Governed System

blocks.p: A diagram becomes an operating architecture only when its runtime contract is explicit. Recommended minimum artifacts are: a role-and-permission registry; a task schema; a routing policy; a versioned artifact/evidence store; a workflow-state ledger; an approval matrix; evaluation datasets; and logs that connect every action to the initiating request.
Table 5 sets out the control loop of a governed orchestrator as language-independent steps, not as an executable library interface.

table.caption: Control loop of a governed orchestrator.
head: Step
Orchestrator action
Control enforced
rows: Create a bounded plan; assign an owner and a budget to every task
Choose a specialist for each runnable task
Run each task with a timeout and save the result as a versioned artifact
Check each result against its task contract and provenance
Combine only verified artifacts into a candidate result
An independent quality gate returns pass, revise or stop

Retry budget; release authority; audit trail
table.note: Step 3 uses a fixed route or a validated bid; the loop is the same for both.

blocks.p: To move toward production, run a four-step pilot. First, measure a single-agent baseline against representative real tasks. Second, implement centralized routing with one or two true specialist boundaries and compare accepted-result quality. Third, add blackboard state, concurrency, or hierarchy only for demonstrated bottlenecks. Fourth, inject failures—timeouts, missing vendor data, contradictory evidence, duplicate messages, and malicious instructions—before enabling any high-impact external actions.
Each task needs a contract, and each coordination mechanism adds fields to it (Table 6). These fields are proposed engineering controls, not universal schemas imposed by a particular framework.

table.caption: Proposed task contract fields.
head: Contract
Fields
rows: task ID, owner, input artifact IDs, expected output schema, allowed tools, deadline, maximum retries, evidence requirements, release status
bid ID, capability evidence, estimated cost, estimated duration, award decision, expiry
artifact version, origin, integrity check, access policy, supersedes reference

sections.title: Evaluation: Decide with Data, Not Architecture Labels

blocks.p: Before declaring a topology better, evaluate it against the same task set, datasets, quality rubrics, model configuration, and external-tool conditions. Include difficult and adversarial tasks; report failed, escalated, and partially completed runs rather than suppressing them. Anthropic's production research account emphasizes end-state evaluation, robust prompt and tool design, and operational discipline [4].

table.caption: Recommended evaluation measures.
head: Metric
Operational definition
Decision relevance
rows: Results passing required evidence and quality gates / attempted tasks
Request to authorized, completed delivery, including queueing and review
Model, tools, infrastructure, reviewer time and retries
Agent messages, LLM turns and duplicate work per accepted result
Fault-injection cases completed without duplicate side effects / recovery attempts
Verified material claims and correctly authorized actions / sampled items
table.note: Priorities and thresholds should reflect business criticality and failure consequences.

blocks.p: Table 4 defines the measures; each is a ratio or total over the same task set.

Compare cost and quality jointly. A faster workflow that produces an unverified recommendation may be worse than a slower one that passes evidence and approval gates. A market-based scheduler that finds a cheaper worker is not beneficial if bidding overhead or rework costs exceed the savings. A blackboard that enables strong team collaboration still requires ownership, correction, and retention policies. Architecture selection is therefore an empirical systems-engineering decision with an explicit operating envelope.

The five-model framework is useful because it exposes different ways agents can cooperate, but the models operate on overlapping design axes. Centralized orchestration emphasizes accountability; hierarchy organizes multiple domains; mesh enables peer communication; blackboard coordinates through shared state; and contract net negotiates task allocation. None independently ensures intelligence, scalability, reliability, or safe autonomy.

For most early enterprise and SME deployments, begin with the smallest architecture that provides measurable value: a responsible lead, constrained specialists, a durable evidence store, and a real verification/release gate. Introduce decentralized routing, deeper hierarchy, or bids only when workload testing demonstrates their benefit. Prefer interoperable and inspectable artifacts to long, unstructured conversational handoffs. Keep permissions, replay, provenance, observability, and human oversight outside the discretion of individual agents.

Pre-release checklist: (1) responsibility and stop conditions documented; (2) task schemas and artifact provenance validated; (3) state and external side effects recoverable; (4) agent identities and tool permissions least-privileged; (5) bounded retries and conflict rules tested; (6) quality metrics compared with a single-agent baseline; and (7) all high-consequence external actions gated by appropriate authorization. These controls matter more than the number of boxes in an architecture diagram.
